landmarks.name: Westin Peachtree Plaza
landmarks.summary: John Portman's mirrored glass cylinder, the tallest hotel in the world when it opened, with a revolving restaurant on top. Its lobby has a half-acre lake.

landmarks.name: CNN Center
landmarks.summary: Ted Turner's headquarters of the round-the-clock Cable News Network and Superstation WTBS. Visitors watch the anchors through the studio glass.

landmarks.name: The Omni
landmarks.summary: The rusting steel arena of the Hawks, where Dominique Wilkins, 'the Human Highlight Film', dunks over everyone. Its weathering steel was meant to rust; the roof was not meant to leak.

landmarks.name: Atlanta-Fulton County Stadium
landmarks.summary: The round stadium of the Braves and Falcons, where Hank Aaron hit his 715th home run in 1974. 'The Launching Pad' for its thin air and short fences.

landmarks.name: Underground Atlanta
landmarks.summary: The old street-level shopping and nightlife district beneath the viaducts, closed and shuttered since 1982. The city is planning to reopen it.

landmarks.name: Fox Theatre
landmarks.summary: The 1929 Moorish movie palace on Peachtree Street with a ceiling of twinkling stars, saved from demolition by a public campaign. Concerts and touring Broadway fill it now.

landmarks.name: Georgia State Capitol
landmarks.summary: The 1889 capitol whose dome is covered in gold leaf from Dahlonega, where America's first gold rush began. The legislature sits each winter.

landmarks.name: Martin Luther King Jr. Center
landmarks.summary: The memorial and centre on Auburn Avenue where Dr. King lies in a tomb in a reflecting pool. His first federal holiday was celebrated this January.

landmarks.name: Ebenezer Baptist Church
landmarks.summary: The church on Auburn Avenue where Martin Luther King Jr., his father and grandfather all preached. Sweet Auburn, around it, was the richest Black street in America.

landmarks.name: The Varsity
landmarks.summary: The world's largest drive-in, serving chili dogs and frosted oranges to Georgia Tech since 1928. 'What'll ya have?' is shouted at every customer.

landmarks.name: Stone Mountain
landmarks.summary: The giant granite dome east of the city, carved with Confederate generals on horseback. A laser show plays across the carving on summer nights.

landmarks.name: Coca-Cola Headquarters
landmarks.summary: The tower of the world's most famous soft drink on North Avenue. Last year's New Coke disaster is still being lived down.

landmarks.name: Piedmont Park
landmarks.summary: The city's big park, laid out for the 1895 Cotton States Exposition, with Lake Clara Meer and views of the Midtown skyline. The Arts Festival fills it every September.

landmarks.name: Georgia Tech
landmarks.summary: The 'Rambling Wreck' engineering school on North Avenue, its Tech Tower spelling T-E-C-H in lights. Students keep stealing the T.

landmarks.name: Hartsfield Atlanta International Airport
landmarks.summary: The busiest airport in the South, with its underground train between concourses. Whether you're going to heaven or hell, you change planes in Atlanta.

landmarks.name: Margaret Mitchell's apartment
landmarks.summary: The run-down Tudor house on Peachtree where Margaret Mitchell wrote Gone With the Wind in a cramped ground-floor flat she called 'the Dump'. Abandoned now and threatened by developers.

landmarks.name: High Museum of Art
landmarks.summary: Richard Meier's gleaming white museum of 1983 on Peachtree Street, its atrium a ramp curving up like the Guggenheim's. The Woodruff Arts Center beside it holds the Atlanta Symphony.

landmarks.name: Hyatt Regency Atlanta
landmarks.summary: John Portman's hotel with the first great atrium lobby of its kind and a blue flying-saucer revolving restaurant on top. Glass elevators climb the inside of its 22 storeys.

1980s.transitNote: MARTA's East-West and North-South lines (shorter than today's) and the airport's Plane Train. The Atlanta Streetcar (2014) and SkyTrain (2009) came later.
